verifications.claim: The Apollo 11 mission landed humans on the moon on July 20, 1969.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'NASA's Apollo 11 mission made history in July 1969 as the first-ever spaceflight to land humans on the moon.' 'whether humankind first stepped on the Moon on 20 July 1969'; R3: 'the first lunar expedition, by N. Armstrong, E. Aldrin, and M. Collins (USA), July 16–24, 1969.' 'Armstrong was the first man to set foot on the moon (July 21, 1969)'
verifications.reasoning: Directly states Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969.

verifications.claim: Apollo missions landed humans on the moon five more times through 1972.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Yes, we really did land on the moon ... six times, to be exact.'; R3: 'the six crewed landings (1969–1972)'
verifications.reasoning: Confirms six total landings (Apollo 11 plus five more) from 1969-1972.

verifications.claim: Over 800 pounds of lunar samples have been analyzed by scientists worldwide.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'more than 380 kilograms of moon rock' (≈838 lbs); R3: 'The Apollo program collected 380 kg (838 lb) of Moon rocks during the six crewed missions. Analyses by scientists worldwide'
verifications.reasoning: 380 kg is 838 lbs, directly over 800 pounds, analyzed worldwide.

verifications.claim: Lunar samples are entirely unique to the lunar environment.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'The Apollo samples are easily distinguishable from both meteorites and Earth rocks in that they show a lack of hydrous alteration products... unique geochemical traits.' 'these rocks could not have been formed under conditions on Earth.'
verifications.reasoning: Describes lunar samples as uniquely distinguishable from Earth rocks and meteorites due to lunar-specific traits.

verifications.claim: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the Apollo landing sites.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'high-definition photos taken by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) of the Apollo landing sites'
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly states LRO photographed Apollo landing sites.

verifications.claim: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographs of the landing sites show the lunar modules.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'captured the Lunar Module descent stages' 'The pictures show the Apollo missions' lunar module descent stages sitting on the moon's surface'
verifications.reasoning: Directly mentions LRO photos showing Lunar Module descent stages.

verifications.claim: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographs of the landing sites show equipment.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'experiment package (ALSEP), Surveyor 3 spacecraft, and astronaut footpaths are all visible.' 'images were released showing five of the six Apollo missions' American flags'
verifications.reasoning: LRO images show ALSEP equipment, flags, and other hardware.

verifications.claim: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographs of the landing sites show astronaut tracks.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'captured the Lunar Module descent stages and the tracks left by the astronauts.' 'tracks made by an astronaut between a science experiment (ALSEP) and the lander.'
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly states LRO photos show astronaut tracks.

verifications.claim: The Soviet Union tracked the Apollo missions.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'The Soviet Union tracked the Apollo missions at the Space Transmissions Corps' 'the Soviets... extensive intelligence network and a formidable scientific community able to analyze NASA data'
verifications.reasoning: Directly confirms Soviet tracking of Apollo missions.

verifications.claim: Independent observatories have used the laser reflectors placed on the moon to measure the distance to Earth.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'retroreflectors (mirrors used as targets for Earth-based tracking lasers)' 'Lick Observatory... McDonald Observatory detected it'
verifications.reasoning: Independent observatories like Lick and McDonald used Apollo-placed retroreflectors for distance measurement.

verifications.claim: Roughly 400,000 people worked on the Apollo projects.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: '400,000 people involved in the Apollo program'; R3: 'more than 400,000 people who worked on the Apollo project'
verifications.reasoning: Exact figure '400,000' or 'more than 400,000' directly matches.

verifications.claim: The moon landing flag was held up by a horizontal rod to keep it extended in the vacuum of space.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'suspended by a rigid arm, which allows it to remain unfurled and stiff in zero gravity.' 'flag with an aluminum arm sewn into the fabric. This arm holds the flag outright'; R3: 'flag was fastened to an Г-shaped rod (see Lunar Flag Assembly)'
verifications.reasoning: Describes horizontal/rigid arm/rod to extend flag in vacuum.

verifications.claim: The moon landing flag appeared wrinkled.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'It was rippled because it had been folded during storage, and the ripples could be mistaken for movement'
verifications.reasoning: Ripples from folding described as wrinkled appearance.

verifications.claim: The moon landing flag moved only when astronauts handled it.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'appears to be waving... the astronauts did not plant a normal flag'; R3: 'It only seemed to flutter when the astronauts were moving it into position.' 'when the astronauts let go of the flagpole, it vibrates briefly but then remains still.'
verifications.reasoning: Movement only from astronaut handling, then still.

verifications.claim: Apollo mission cameras were set to take photos of the bright lunar surface in daylight.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'could not function at an aperture that allowed them to capture both the stars and the brightly illuminated lunar surface.'; R3: 'cameras used for imaging subjects illuminated by sunlight are set for a daylight exposure.' 'All crewed landings happened during the lunar daytime.'
verifications.reasoning: Cameras set for bright daylight lunar surface.

verifications.claim: Apollo mission cameras could not capture faint stars in the background.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'due to the aperture of the cameras used... any picture that was able to capture the small amounts of light from stars would not be able to clearly picture the astronauts'; R3: 'The dim light of the stars simply does not provide enough exposure'; R4: 'your camera's shutter speed needs to be fast and your aperture incredibly small. In that situation, faint objects like stars simply aren't going to show up.'
verifications.reasoning: Camera settings for bright surface prevent capturing faint stars.

verifications.claim: Non-parallel shadows were caused by the uneven, highly reflective lunar surface.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'lunar soil is distinctly different... partially reflective. This diffuses the light coming from the sun, altering the appearance and placement of shadows'; R3: 'Shadows on the Moon are complicated by reflected light, uneven ground, wide-angle lens distortion, and lunar dust.'
verifications.reasoning: Reflective lunar surface and uneven ground cause non-parallel shadows.

verifications.claim: Apollo astronauts passed through the Van Allen belts quickly.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'passed through the inner belt in a matter of minutes and the outer belt in about 1+1⁄2 hours.'; R4: 'the transit time through the Van Allen radiation belt right at the beginning of the Apollo voyages was incredibly short.'
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly states quick passage through belts.

verifications.claim: Passing through the Van Allen belts quickly minimized astronauts' radiation exposure
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'the orbital transfer trajectory from Earth to the Moon through the belts was chosen to lessen radiation exposure.' 'average dose of less than 1 rem'; R4: 'as long as you walk across quite quickly... you are not going to have enough thermal energy... You’re absolutely fine.' (analogy for radiation)
verifications.reasoning: Quick transit chosen to minimize exposure, doses safe.
